purpose: Coordinate scheduled and event-driven workflows with declarative configuration.
when: Weeks 45-48, after GitLab CI, cloud identity and incident handling
rationale: Use it to study durable operational automation: retries, timeouts, idempotency and partial failure. A second workflow platform is unnecessary until the GitLab delivery pipeline and basic scheduled jobs are understood.
exercise: Build a disposable backup-validation workflow with an explicit timeout, bounded retries and a failure notification to a local test receiver. Trigger the same input twice and prove it cannot overwrite a good backup or create duplicate side effects. Produce a workflow diagram and failure timeline.
evidence: The README describes YAML workflows and retry/error-handling primitives. The sampled Compose file uses PostgreSQL, persistent storage and a health dependency; its comments explicitly identify root access to the Docker socket as a development configuration.
limitations: Do not copy the quick start into production: it uses mutable image tags, sample database credentials and Docker socket access. Enterprise features and community features differ. Workflow success is not proof that the business result is correct.

purpose: Schedule database backups and validate restores.
when: Weeks 23-24 first restore exercise; weeks 41-44 recovery comparison
rationale: The useful lesson is recoverability, not operating a backup dashboard. Start with a manual PostgreSQL dump and restore, then compare what automation adds and what it cannot prove.
exercise: Seed a disposable database with known records, back it up, deliberately remove only the lab database, restore into a separate clean instance, and run application-level assertions. Record measured recovery time, missing transactions, retention behavior and encryption-key recovery steps.
evidence: The README documents logical and physical backups, WAL/PITR support, retention settings and restore verification. It also warns that the application's encryption key must be backed up to recover encrypted backups.
limitations: A successful restore job or row count does not prove application consistency. Protect backup credentials and encryption keys separately; keep tests isolated from real data. CI/security assurances in the README were read, not independently reproduced.

purpose: Emulate AWS interfaces locally for development and automated integration tests.
when: Weeks 7-8 test isolation; repeat against real AWS in weeks 13-16
rationale: Use one narrowly scoped storage or queue integration to learn endpoint injection and reproducible fixtures. The local emulator keeps the rapid feedback loop inexpensive; real-cloud checks establish the compatibility boundary.
exercise: Write upload/download and missing-object tests against isolated S3 emulation. Inject the endpoint through configuration, use fake local credentials and clean up fixtures. Later run the same contract suite against a temporary AWS bucket, including an explicit access-denied case, and document differences.
evidence: The README includes AWS SDK endpoint configuration and Python, Java and Node Testcontainers examples. It says default credentials can be arbitrary non-empty values unless stricter checks are enabled, and some service modes start real Docker containers.
limitations: Passing emulator tests does not validate real IAM, regional behavior, quotas, networking, billing or managed-service availability. Do not claim complete AWS parity from the supported-service list. Avoid mounting the Docker socket unless the chosen test requires it.

purpose: Automate Apple application release workflows through a command-line interface.
when: Weeks 45-48 reading exercise; implementation only for a mobile platform role
rationale: This is a specialization, not a missing prerequisite for AWS/GCP DevOps. Extract reusable release-engineering ideas without buying Apple tooling or building an unrelated application.
exercise: Read the release workflow and draft a generic GitLab release-job checklist: validate inputs, pin dependencies, use machine-readable output, protect signing material, require a release approval and clean temporary credentials. Apply those principles to the existing container release.
evidence: The README documents structured output, authentication diagnostics and release automation. The CI guide includes GitLab components, fresh macOS-runner signing steps and an AWS workload-identity example for object storage.
limitations: Real mobile signing and release work has platform/account prerequisites and can publish externally. The inspected CI snippets use floating refs; pin reviewed versions in your own examples. The README documents default usage telemetry.

purpose: Self-host Git collaboration, code review, packages and automation.
rationale: Use its operational documentation to understand the responsibilities hidden by hosted source control. Keep GitLab as the primary delivery platform; use a disposable Gitea instance only if time remains.
exercise: Write a source-control service recovery plan covering repositories, database, attachments, configuration and credentials. Optionally restore a throwaway instance and prove a clone, commit history and issue attachment survive. Compare the maintenance burden with the GitLab service used in the course.
evidence: The README describes an integrated development service with GitHub-Actions-compatible CI. The backup documentation explains that database, files and repositories can become inconsistent and instructs stopping the instance for its documented consistent backup procedure.
limitations: A Git repository mirror is not a complete platform backup. Gitea Actions syntax and runner behavior do not teach GitLab CI directly. Avoid expanding this comparison into a second permanent CI platform.

purpose: Observe host, container and service resource behavior.
when: Weeks 3-4 applied Linux diagnosis; revisit weeks 33-36
rationale: Its immediate feedback helps connect processes and kernel counters to application latency. Use it for a short diagnosis lab, then retain only the observability stack selected for the capstone.
exercise: Create controlled CPU pressure and a slow-disk scenario inside a disposable VM. Correlate latency with CPU, memory, disk and network charts and verify the diagnosis with Linux tools. Write a two-page incident note containing the failed hypothesis as well as the final cause.
evidence: The README describes collection, storage and alerting in the Agent and lists host/container monitoring. The security/privacy documentation distinguishes observability data from metadata sent to Cloud and documents anonymous usage statistics.
limitations: A dashboard does not supply an SLO or prove causality. Measure collector overhead in the lab rather than accepting marketing performance claims. Review dashboard exposure, host access and telemetry settings; Agent, UI and Cloud have different licensing and service boundaries.

purpose: Operate a self-hosted application deployment platform.
when: Weeks 45-48, after manual VM/container delivery and Kubernetes
rationale: Study the developer experience a platform team should provide: repeatable deployment, logs, backups and rollback. Compare those conveniences with the infrastructure and operational responsibilities underneath.
exercise: Trace the deployment of the capstone app on paper: source, image build, registry, secrets, routing, storage, health checks and recovery. Produce an architecture decision record comparing your GitLab/Terraform/Ansible path with Dokploy; optionally repeat on a disposable VM.
evidence: The README describes Docker Compose, Docker Swarm multi-node operation, Traefik routing and backups. The inspected license file applies Apache 2.0 outside a proprietary-directory carve-out.
limitations: Swarm-based operation is not Kubernetes practice. One-click deployment does not establish backup correctness, least privilege or high availability. The installer is powerful host-changing code; inspect and pin a release before any future lab execution.

purpose: Connect application errors and performance problems to code changes.
when: Weeks 33-36, after basic logs, metrics and tracing
rationale: Use one instrumented service to learn release attribution and safe error reporting. Running a full Sentry platform is a separate operating challenge and is not required to learn the concept.
exercise: Introduce a controlled exception in staging, attach release/environment metadata, diagnose it from the recorded event, ship a fix and verify the regression test. Demonstrate that a fake password and access token are removed before telemetry leaves the process.
evidence: The README links language SDKs for error debugging. The self-hosted repository describes its package as intended for low-volume deployments and proofs of concept. The current main-repository license identifies FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0.
limitations: Do not treat the whole repository as permissively licensed open source. Error events can carry sensitive application data. The self-hosted documentation site was unavailable during this inspection; no resource sizing or deployment reliability was verified.

purpose: Run supported GitHub Actions workflows locally using containers.
rationale: Learn the distinction between a local job rehearsal and a provider's control plane. Your target is GitLab, so the main exercise belongs in GitLab's own pipeline validation and real runner execution.
exercise: Read one simple upstream GitHub workflow and translate its lint/test/build intent into GitLab jobs. Write a parity table for jobs, artifacts, caches, identity, approvals and concurrency. Optionally use act only on a reviewed workflow with fake credentials.
evidence: The README says act reads .github/workflows and runs through Docker. Its limitations page says job permissions, environment scoping, concurrency and several timeout behaviors are ignored, and OIDC URLs are not provided.
limitations: act is not a GitLab CI emulator. A successful local run cannot validate hosted authorization, environment approvals or deployment concurrency. Workflows execute code with the access you grant the runner; inspect them before running.

purpose: Reconcile Kubernetes application state from version-controlled desired configuration.
when: Weeks 29-32, after Kubernetes workloads, networking, storage and RBAC
rationale: This is a strong fit once you can deploy and troubleshoot the app manually. GitLab remains responsible for validation and building the artifact; Argo CD teaches continuous reconciliation and controlled promotion.
exercise: Have GitLab publish an immutable image and propose its digest in an environment repository. Review and merge, observe reconciliation, introduce a harmless replica-count drift, compare self-heal off/on, and revert a bad release through Git. Save timeline evidence and a rollback runbook.
evidence: The README defines Argo CD as Kubernetes GitOps delivery. The auto-sync documentation distinguishes sync, self-healing and pruning; pruning is disabled by default, and direct rollback is unavailable while automated sync is enabled.
limitations: Pruning can delete resources and self-heal can overwrite emergency manual edits. Start in an isolated namespace with restrictive access. A Git revert of application manifests does not reverse an incompatible database migration.

purpose: Trace processes, ports and containers back to their launch chain.
when: Weeks 1-4 diagnostic validation; repeat during incident drills
rationale: Use it as a cross-check after solving the same mystery with native tools. The lasting skill is reasoning about processes, service managers, parent-child relationships and namespaces.
exercise: Create a harmless service that keeps restarting and a second service with a port conflict. Identify the owner and launch chain using ps, ss, lsof and systemctl, then compare witr's report. Deliver a runbook that fixes the service definition instead of repeatedly killing a child process.
evidence: The README documents process/port/container tracing, JSON output and a TUI. Its platform matrix and permissions section describe visibility differences and elevated access requirements; the TUI also includes process actions.
limitations: Treat diagnostic output as sensitive because environment and process details may contain secrets. Use inspection operations only during the first exercise; TUI process actions are not read-only. Windows and WSL visibility differ from a Linux server.

purpose: Keep structured configuration encrypted while managing who can decrypt it.
when: Weeks 11-12 local age lab; weeks 17-20 AWS KMS; weeks 37-40 GCP KMS
rationale: It connects Git hygiene, identity and cloud key management without requiring a large secrets platform. Learn the difference between encrypting a file, authorizing decryption and rotating the underlying application secret.
exercise: Encrypt fake configuration with age and prove an unauthorized key cannot decrypt it. Later use a tightly scoped cloud identity with KMS, test a denied identity, rotate a recipient, and recover using an approved backup identity. Verify plaintext never appears in CI logs or retained artifacts.
evidence: The README lists structured formats and AWS KMS, GCP KMS, age and other key backends. The official docs expose usage and security-model sections; the repository includes examples and functional-test directories.
limitations: Encryption at rest does not protect plaintext after decryption. Removing a recipient cannot erase old Git history or revoke a secret already seen; rotate the actual secret when access is lost. Do not assume Argo CD automatically decrypts SOPS files without a reviewed integration.

purpose: Explore application telemetry through OpenTelemetry logs, metrics and traces.
when: Weeks 33-36 observability; choose one backend for the capstone
rationale: Make the transferable skill OpenTelemetry instrumentation and diagnosis. Use SigNoz as one possible backend rather than maintaining several overlapping observability products for a one-person course.
exercise: Instrument an HTTP request and a database call, propagate a trace identifier, inject a slow query and locate the latency in a trace. Correlate the trace with a structured log and an error-rate metric, then set a justified sampling and retention policy.
evidence: The README describes an OpenTelemetry-based platform with logs, metrics, traces and alerts, with community and enterprise offerings. The license applies MIT terms outside specified enterprise directories and third-party components.
limitations: Telemetry volume, retention and cardinality consume real storage and compute. Do not assume enterprise access controls exist in the community edition. Redact sensitive attributes before export and keep the ingestion endpoint private.

purpose: Run synthetic endpoint checks and report service status.
when: Weeks 7-8 basic checks; weeks 33-36 external monitoring
rationale: It makes the distinction between a running process and a working user journey concrete. Begin with one simple HTTP contract; later place checks outside the application's failure domain.
exercise: Check status code, expected response content and a justified latency threshold. Break DNS, return a misleading HTTP 200 and stop the app in separate drills. Prove each failure is detected, recovery clears it, and notification thresholds avoid repeated noise.
evidence: The README provides HTTP/TCP/DNS checks, conditions, alerts, authentication and deployment examples. The sampled GitHub test workflow builds the binary and runs Go tests with the race detector; ICMP testing requires elevation in that workflow.
limitations: Synthetic checks complement rather than replace unit, integration and whole-system tests. A monitor inside the same failed cluster may vanish with the app. Keep credentials out of public check output, and do not make alpha workflow suites a core dependency.

purpose: Discover categorized system-administration tools and their upstream projects.
when: Weeks 1-52, only when answering a specific operational need
rationale: Treat it as a directory for comparing options, not a syllabus or installation queue. It is useful when you can state the problem, constraints and acceptance criteria before opening a category.
exercise: Choose a genuine requirement, such as configuration management or external monitoring. Compare three candidates on maintenance, licensing, access control, backup/recovery, resource costs and integration effort. Write a one-page decision record that explains why you rejected two.
evidence: The README groups projects into categories including configuration management, CI/CD, backup and monitoring; entries provide upstream links and license/language labels. It includes Ansible, GitLab CI and Argo CD in the inspected sections.
limitations: Directory inclusion is not a security audit or proof that a project is still maintained. Follow the upstream documentation and verify the current license/version before adopting a tool. Limit browsing so it does not replace building and debugging.
